extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates or graduate students studying commutative algebra; instructors/solvers of textbook exercises
extracted.subtask_description: Solutions and explanatory notes for textbook exercises in commutative algebra (primary decomposition, length, Hilbert functions, graded modules, dimension, completion, DVR-related facts). Contains statements, equivalences, and constructions used to test algebraic properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary ideal (power condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal q is primary if whenever xy ∈ q and x ∉ q then y^n ∈ q for some n ≥ 1 (equivalently: if xy ∈ q and x ∉ √q then y ∈ q up to a power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly (cited as (18.5)). In proofs, to show inverse images or components are primary one shows that if product falls in ideal and first factor not in radical then some power of second factor lies in the ideal. Example: in verifying an ideal is primary one shows φ(x)φ(y) ∈ q and φ(x) ∉ q ⇒ φ(y)^n ∈ q, hence y^n in φ^{-1}(q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse image of primary under ring homomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ: R → R' is a ring homomorphism and q ⊆ R' is p-primary, then φ^{-1}(q) ⊆ R is φ^{-1}(p)-primary. Conversely, if φ is surjective then primaryness descends/pulls back in the opposite direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses: if xy ∈ φ^{-1}(q) but x ∉ φ^{-1}(q) then φ(x)φ(y) ∈ q and φ(x) ∉ q, so φ(y)^n ∈ q and y^n ∈ φ^{-1}(q). The converse is similar when φ is surjective (exercise (18.8)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Irredundant primary decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A representation a = ⋂_{i=1}^n q_i with each q_i primary is irredundant if no q_i can be omitted; associated primes pi = √q_i are recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction and verification: show inclusion both ways; show q1 and q2 distinct primes so decomposition is irredundant (example (18.16)). Irredundancy used in uniqueness/Ass(R) considerations (e.g., (18.27)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime ideals are primary
rubrics_metrics.description: Every prime ideal p is p-primary (i.e., primary ideals include primes as special cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify components being primary when they are prime ideals (cited (17.4), (2.11)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadratic-stability condition for the example ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal a = ⟨X^2, XY⟩ in k[X,Y] satisfies: if ab^2 ∈ a then a^2 ⊆ a or b^2 ⊆ a (exercise (18.7)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a special property to check for the given ideal: use factorization and membership checks to deduce whether powers of factors lie in a; shows a is not primary though its radical may be prime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic power defined as saturation
rubrics_metrics.description: The nth symbolic power p^{(n)} is defined as the saturation (p^n)S where S = R \ p (localization away from p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the p-primary component of p^n (exercise (18.26)(1)). Used to relate ordinary powers and symbolic powers and to identify primary components via localization/saturation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic power properties (additivity, equality, containment)
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) p^{(n)} is the p-primary component of p^n. (2) p^{(m+n)} is the p-primary component of p^{(m)} p^{(n)}. (3) p^{(n)} = p^n iff p^n is p-primary. (4) For any p-primary ideal q, q ⊆ p^{(n)} for all large n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use localization, support/Ass arguments, and saturation facts ((11.15)(3), (18.24), (18.26)(4)). These are practical tests for when ordinary and symbolic powers agree and for primary component containment for large powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submodule supported on V(a): a(M) characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finitely generated module M and ideal a, a(M) := { m ∈ M | a^n m = 0 for some n } equals the set of m whose support lies in V(a) (i.e., m localized at primes not containing a vanishes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shown by comparing with components in an irredundant primary decomposition of 0 in M (exercise (18.21)). Useful to detect sections of a module supported inside a closed subscheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstructing N from localizations at associated primes
rubrics_metrics.description: If N ⊆ M and M is finitely generated over Noetherian ring R, then N = ⋂_{p ∈ Ass(M/N)} φ_p^{-1}(N_p) (exercise (18.25) formulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses a submodule as intersection of inverse images of its localized pieces at associated primes, giving a canonical decomposition in terms of Ass(M/N). Useful when proving equalities of submodules via localization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary decomposition of zero in a product of domains
rubrics_metrics.description: If R = R' × R'' (product of two domains), then ⟨0⟩ = p' ∩ p'' where p' = ⟨0⟩ × R'' and p'' = R' × ⟨0⟩; these are prime (hence primary) and the decomposition is irredundant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete example showing how zero decomposes in product rings (exercise (18.17)); used as a test/example of primary decomposition behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-uniqueness of primary decompositions when associated prime not minimal
rubrics_metrics.description: If p_i is not minimal among associated primes, then replacing the corresponding q_i by p_i^{(r)} for large r produces infinitely many distinct irredundant primary decompositions of ⟨0⟩ (exercise (18.27)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction uses localizing at p_i and Nakayama to obtain distinct p_i-primary ideals p_i^{(r)} for large r; demonstrates source of non-uniqueness in primary decomposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple module characterization and annihilator
rubrics_metrics.description: M is simple ⇔ M ≅ R/m for some maximal ideal m; in that case m = Ann(M). Any nonzero element of a simple module generates it (exercise (19.2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to recognize simple modules and to compute lengths and composition factors; basic test for simplicity in module-theoretic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite length module equivalences
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Noetherian ring R and finitely generated module M, the following are equivalent: (1) M has finite length; (2) Supp(M) consists entirely of maximal ideals; (3) Ass(M) consists entirely of maximal ideals. Moreover, then Ass(M) = Supp(M) is finite (exercise (19.4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These equivalences let one test finite length via support or associated primes; applies to verify Artinian/Noetherian interplay and to count composition factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chains of primary ideals bounded by module length
rubrics_metrics.description: For R Noetherian, q a p-primary ideal, chains of p-primary ideals from q to p have length at most ℓ(A) where A := (R/q)_p, and maximal chains have length exactly ℓ(A) (exercise (19.5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correspondence via quotient and localization reduces the question to the Artinian local case; useful for comparing lengths of primary chains with module length invariants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert series vs Hilbert polynomial distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Two graded ideals can have different Hilbert series but the same Hilbert polynomial (example: ⟨X, Y^2⟩ and ⟨X^2, Y^2⟩ in k[X,Y]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that Hilbert polynomial captures asymptotic growth (degree and leading coefficient) but not initial graded behavior; used to caution against equating series and polynomial invariants (exercise (20.5)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Largest homogeneous submodule with same Hilbert polynomial
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a homogeneous submodule N of a graded module M, define N' = { m ∈ M | ∃k0 so R_k m ⊆ N for all k ≥ k0 }; N' is the largest homogeneous submodule of M containing N with the same Hilbert polynomial (exercise (20.6), (20.23)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: take homogeneous generators of N' and find degree bound after which graded pieces agree; N' characterized as preimage of (0 :_{M/N} R_+) in graded context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree change of Hilbert polynomial on killing a homogeneous nonzerodivisor power
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ∈ R is homogeneous nonzerodivisor and Mf=0 (or f^kM = 0), then deg h(M;n) > deg h(R;n) (concrete computation for M = R/⟨f^k⟩ shows shift and degree comparison) (exercise (20.10)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to exact sequence 0 → R(-c) → R → M → 0 for R/⟨f^k⟩; degree and leading coefficient comparisons follow from additivity of Hilbert functions and standard polynomial shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artin–Rees lemma ⇒ Krull Intersection Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: The Artin–Rees lemma for a-adic filtrations implies the Krull Intersection Theorem: ⋂_{n≥0} (a^n M) = 0 under appropriate hypotheses (exercise (20.19)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Artin–Rees to submodule N and a-adic filtration to deduce stabilization and hence intersection triviality; practical method to deduce Krull intersection from filtration control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneity of natural constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: In a graded ring/module setting, a homogeneous ideal a and constructions Ann(M) and nil(M) are homogeneous ideals/submodules (exercise (20.25)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: check homogeneous components separately; if x ∈ Ann(M) then each homogeneous component annihilates homogeneous generators. Useful to ensure grading preserved under standard module/ideal operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneous part of a primary submodule is primary
rubrics_metrics.description: If Q ⊆ M is a primary submodule in a graded module M, then Q^{hom} (submodule generated by homogeneous elements of Q) is primary as well (exercise (20.26)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: test homogeneous x, m with xm ∈ Q^{hom} and use primaryness of Q together with degree arguments to conclude m ∈ Q^{hom}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral closure localization and Hilbert polynomial invariance
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is a graded domain whose integral closure R is finitely generated as R-module, then there exists homogeneous f with R_f = R_f and the Hilbert polynomials of R and R have the same degree and leading coefficient (exercise (20.30)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct f clearing denominators of finite module generators; deduce vanishing of R/R after localization and apply degree comparison lemmas for Hilbert polynomials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Krull Principal Ideal Theorem and dimension consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is prime minimal over a principal ideal (x), then ht(p) = 1. Consequences include: primes minimal over nonzero elements of domain have height 1; dim(R[X]) = dim(R) + 1 (exercise (21.16)); chains in quotients by principal elements drop appropriate length (exercise (21.14)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use principal ideal theorem and localization to compute heights and compare dimensions; applicable in arguments about chains of primes and Krull dimension behavior under polynomial extension and quotients.

rubrics_metrics.name: UFD and height-1 prime correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is a UFD then every height-1 prime is principal. Conversely, if R is Noetherian and every height-1 prime is principal, then R is a UFD (exercise (21.12)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor nonzero elements into irreducibles and use minimal primes over factors; conversely, verify irreducible elements are prime using principalness of corresponding height-1 primes and Noetherian hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular local ring criteria via m/m^2
rubrics_metrics.description: For Noetherian local ring A of dimension r with maximal ideal m, r ≤ dim_k(m/m^2) with equality iff m can be generated by r elements and A is regular. Regularity equivalently characterized via existence of regular system of parameters (exercises (21.17), (21.21)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parameter ideals, minimal number of generators of m, and relations between dimension and generators; practical test for regularity is computing dimension of m/m^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion preserves Noetherian/local/dimension/regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: For Noetherian local ring A with maximal ideal m, the m-adic completion bA is Noetherian local with maximal ideal bm, dim(A) = dim(bA), and A is regular ⇔ bA is regular (exercise (22.28)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses properties of completions, identification of quotients A/m^n ≅ bA/bm^n, and comparison of m/m^2 with bm/bm^2 to transfer generator counts (hence regularity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion detects nonzerodivisors under semilocal hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: If x ∈ A is a nonzerodivisor then its image bx in the completion bA is a nonzerodivisor. Conversely, if A is semilocal and bx is a nonzerodivisor in bA then x is a nonzerodivisor in A (exercise (22.15)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Injectivity of multiplication maps is preserved under completion; conversely use injectivity on image of A in bA (which is injective for semilocal Jacobson-radical completion) to lift property back to A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associated graded domain ⇒ completed ring domain (and Krull intersection use)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the associated graded ring Ga(R) is a domain then the completion bR is a domain; if additionally ⋂ a^n = 0 then R injects into bR so R is a domain (exercise (22.10)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue using graded pieces and images in Ga(R) to show nonzero product would give nonzero graded product; apply Krull Intersection to ensure R ↪ bR when intersection vanishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nakayama for complete rings (lifting generators)
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is complete and M is separated, then elements m1,...,mn ∈ M whose images generate M/aM generate M (exercise (22.24)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One can view generators in associated graded and lift using completeness; alternate argument uses surjectivity of canonical map R → bR and Nakayama over bR since ba is contained in Jacobson radical.

rubrics_metrics.name: p-adic completion need not be right-exact (counterexample)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequence of modules built from Z/p^n shows that p-adic completion is not right-exact: natural sequence 0 → bA → bB → b(B/A) need not be exact at bB (exercise (22.16) concrete example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct A = ∏_{n≥1} Z/p and B = ∏_{n≥1} Z/p^n with maps, compute induced completions and observe failure of exactness to caution about functorial limits and completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion of semilocal rings: maximal ideals and radical behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is semilocal with maximal ideals m_1,...,m_t and m = rad(A), then bA is semilocal, its maximal ideals are b m_i, and rad(bA) = b m (exercise (22.12)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use identifications of quotients and inverse limits to match maximal ideals and radicals after completion; important when analyzing decomposition of completed rings and their spectra.

rubrics_metrics.name: M-sequence (two-element) solvability characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: If x,y form an M-sequence (i.e., x is nonzerodivisor on M and y is nonzerodivisor on M/xM) then whenever x m = y n there exists p ∈ M with m = y p and n = x p. Conversely, for local Noetherian rings and x,y in maximal ideal, this solvability criterion implies x,y form an M-sequence (exercise (23.6)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use residues in M/xM and divisibility tests by z-divisors; iterative argument with Noetherian hypothesis gives converse by showing eventual vanishing via stabilization and Nakayama-type unit arguments.
